headline: The Paycheck Fairness Act would have strengthened federal rules against paying men and women differently for equal work, but the Senate did not take it up and it was not adopted.
what_it_does: If adopted, this bill would have changed the Equal Pay Act so that an employer's pay difference based on factors other than sex would have to be a bona fide factor like education, training, or experience, tied to the job and a business necessity. It would have let workers recover compensatory damages, and punitive damages against non-government employers, and allowed class actions. It would also have barred employers from punishing workers who discuss or disclose their pay, and required the EEOC to collect pay data by sex, race, and national origin.

who_it_affects.group: Women and men employed in jobs where pay differences exist
who_it_affects.how: They would have gained stronger legal tools to challenge pay gaps between sexes for similar work.
They would have faced tighter limits on pay-difference defenses, possible damages for violations, and new pay data reporting to the EEOC.

who_it_affects.group: Employees who ask about, discuss, or share their wages
who_it_affects.how: They would have been protected from employer retaliation for those actions.
They would have been exempt from punitive damages but still subject to the other pay-equity rules.
They would have received Labor Department and EEOC technical assistance materials to help them comply.

who_it_affects.group: Girls and women seeking negotiation skills
who_it_affects.how: They could have become eligible for training programs funded by Labor Department grants.
